fanoutqa_016178.x:
Bill Gates :: Early life and education :: part 02 :: chunk_0004
In 1971, a Lakeside teacher enlisted Gates and Evans to automate the school's class-scheduling system, providing them computer time and royalties in return. The duo worked diligently in order to have the program ready for their senior year. Towards the end of their junior year, Evans was killed in a mountain climbing accident, which Gates described as one of the saddest days of his life. He then turned to Allen, who helped him finish the system for Lakeside.[[7]](#cite_note-leibovich20001231-8)

At age 17, Gates formed a venture with Allen called [Traf-O-Data](/wiki/Traf-O-Data "Traf-O-Data") to make traffic counters based on the [Intel 8008](/wiki/Intel_8008 "Intel 8008") processor.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGates199614-20) In 1972, he served as a [congressional page](/wiki/Congressional_page "Congressional page") in the House of Representatives.[[20]](#cite_note-Schuman2008-21)[[21]](#cite_note-Sims2018-22) He was a [national merit scholar](/wiki/National_Merit_Scholarship_Program "National Merit Scholarship Program") when he graduated from Lakeside School in 1973.[[22]](#cite_note-23) He scored 1590 out of 1600 on the [Scholastic Aptitude Tests](/wiki/SAT "SAT") (SAT) and enrolled at [Harvard University](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") in the autumn of 1973.[[23]](#cite_note-24)[[24]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGates199615-25)

Gates did not stay at Harvard long enough to choose a concentration, but took mathematics (including [Math 55](/wiki/Math_55 "Math 55")) and graduate-level computer science courses.[[25]](#cite_note-26) While at Harvard, he met fellow student and future Microsoft CEO [Steve Ballmer](/wiki/Steve_Ballmer "Steve Ballmer"). Gates left Harvard after two years while Ballmer stayed and graduated *[magna cum laude](/wiki/Magna_cum_laude "Magna cum laude")*. Years later, Ballmer succeeded Gates as Microsoft's CEO and maintained that position from 2000 until his resignation in 201

fanoutqa_002098.t: Pancreatic cancer :: Risk factors :: Alcohol :: chunk_0009
fanoutqa_002098.x:
Pancreatic cancer :: Risk factors :: Alcohol :: chunk_0009
Main article: [Alcohol abuse](/wiki/Alcohol_abuse "Alcohol abuse")

Drinking alcohol excessively is a major cause of [chronic pancreatitis](/wiki/Chronic_pancreatitis "Chronic pancreatitis"), which in turn predisposes to pancreatic cancer, but considerable research has failed to firmly establish alcohol consumption as a direct risk factor for pancreatic cancer. Overall, the association is consistently weak and the majority of studies have found no association, with smoking a strong [confounding](/wiki/Confounding "Confounding") factor. The evidence is stronger for a link with heavy drinking, of at least six drinks per day.[[3]](#cite_note-Wolfgang2013-3)[[55]](#cite_note-Pericleous-55)

fanoutqa_000818.x:
Ko Wen-je :: 2024 presidential campaign :: Talks with KMT :: chunk_0011
On 15 November 2023, TPP and KMT leadership announced a plan to field a single joint presidential ticket consisting of Ko and KMT candidate [Hou Yu-ih](/wiki/Hou_Yu-ih "Hou Yu-ih"), with the order to be determined by opinion polls and publicly announced on 18 November.[[91]](#cite_note-95) However, Ko was unable to come to an agreement with the KMT leadership, and on 19 November he publicly affirmed that he still intended to run as the presidential candidate of the TPP.[[92]](#cite_note-96) Speculation continued until the filing deadline on 24 November, when Ko registered his candidacy along with his running mate [Cynthia Wu](/wiki/Cynthia_Wu "Cynthia Wu").[[93]](#cite_note-97)

On 13 January 2024, Ko received 26.46% of the popular vote.[[94]](#cite_note-:19-98) Ko conceded the presidential election to [Lai Ching-te](/wiki/Lai_Ching-te "Lai Ching-te"), stating that the TPP had shown that Taiwan was no longer dominated by the [Pan-Blue](/wiki/Pan-Blue_coalition "Pan-Blue coalition") or [Pan-Green coalitions](/wiki/Pan-Green_coalition "Pan-Green coalition").[[95]](#cite_note-99)

Rivest's 1974 doctoral dissertation concerned the use of [hash tables](/wiki/Hash_table "Hash table") to quickly match [partial words](/wiki/Partial_word "Partial word") in documents; he later published this work as a journal paper.[[A3]](#CITEREFA3) His research from this time on [self-organizing lists](/wiki/Self-organizing_list "Self-organizing list")[[A4]](#CITEREFA4) became one of the important precursors to the development of [competitive analysis](/wiki/Competitive_analysis_(online_algorithm) "Competitive analysis (online algorithm)") for [online algorithms](/wiki/Online_algorithm "Online algorithm").[[15]](#cite_note-15) In the early 1980s, he also published well-cited research on two-dimensional [bin packing problems](/wiki/Bin_packing_problem "Bin packing problem"),[[A5]](#CITEREFA5) and on [channel routing](/wiki/Channel_routing "Channel routing") in [VLSI design](/wiki/VLSI_design "VLSI design").[[A6]](#CITEREFA6)

fanoutqa_009522.x:
Jupiter :: Orbital motion and observation :: chunk_0015
Jupiter is the only planet whose [barycentre](/wiki/Barycentre "Barycentre") with the Sun lies outside the volume of the Sun, though by 7% of the Sun's radius.[[133]](#cite_note-139)[[134]](#cite_note-Jupiter-COM-20160730-140) The average distance between Jupiter and the Sun is 778 million km (5.20 AU) and it completes an orbit every 11.86 years. This is approximately two-fifths the orbital period of Saturn, forming a near [orbital resonance](/wiki/Orbital_resonance "Orbital resonance").[[135]](#cite_note-141) The [orbital plane](/wiki/Orbital_plane "Orbital plane") of Jupiter is [inclined](/wiki/Orbital_inclination "Orbital inclination") 1.30° compared to Earth. Because the [eccentricity](/wiki/Orbital_eccentricity "Orbital eccentricity") of its orbit is 0.049, Jupiter is slightly over 75 million km nearer the Sun at [perihelion](/wiki/Perihelion "Perihelion") than [aphelion](/wiki/Aphelion "Aphelion"),[[3]](#cite_note-fact-5) which means that its orbit is nearly circular. This low eccentricity is at odds with [exoplanet](/wiki/Exoplanet "Exoplanet") discoveries, which have revealed Jupiter-sized planets with very high eccentricities. Models suggest this may be due to there being two giant planets in the Solar System, as the presence of a third or more giant planets tends to induce larger eccentricities.[[136]](#cite_note-142)

James Monroe :: Secretary of State and Secretary of War (1811–1817) :: Election of 1816 :: chunk_0018
Main article: [1816 United States presidential election](/wiki/1816_United_States_presidential_election "1816 United States presidential election")

Monroe decided to seek the presidency in the 1816 election, and his war-time leadership had established him as Madison's heir apparent. Monroe had strong support from many in the party, but his candidacy was challenged at the 1816 Democratic-Republican [congressional nominating caucus](/wiki/Congressional_nominating_caucus "Congressional nominating caucus"). Since there was no longer a serious opposition party due to the decline of the Federalists, who were perceived as disloyal due to their pro-British stance and opposition to the War of 1812, the Democratic-Republican caucus in Congress was crucial to Monroe's victory.[[83]](#cite_note-84) Secretary of the Treasury [William H. Crawford](/wiki/William_H._Crawford "William H. Crawford") had the support of numerous Southern and Western Congressmen, while Governor [Daniel D. Tompkins](/wiki/Daniel_D._Tompkins "Daniel D. Tompkins") was backed by several Congressmen from New York. Crawford appealed especially to many Democratic-Republicans who were wary of Madison and Monroe's support for the establishment of the Second Bank of the United States.[[84]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECunningham199615–16-85) Despite his substantial backing, Crawford decided to defer to Monroe on the belief that he could eventually run as Monroe's successor, and Monroe won his party's nomination. Tompkins won the party's vice presidential nomination. The moribund Federalists nominated Rufus King as their presidential nominee, but the party offered little opposition following the conclusion of a popular war that they had opposed. 57th Annual Grammy Awards :: Changes :: chunk_0032
As usual, had a number of small changes in the voting and awarding process:

* New categories

The [Best American Roots Performance](/wiki/Best_American_Roots_Performance "Best American Roots Performance") is a new category in the American Roots genre field. It was presented to the creators of the best performance in this genre field, which includes traditional Northern American (or *regional roots*) musical styles such as [cajun](/wiki/Cajun "Cajun"), [zydeco](/wiki/Zydeco "Zydeco"), [polka](/wiki/Polka "Polka") and others.
Another new category is the [Best Roots Gospel Album](/wiki/Best_Roots_Gospel_Album "Best Roots Gospel Album") in the Gospel genre field, for gospel albums in the aforementioned musical styles, including traditional southern Gospel music.

* Changes in the Gospel categories

The Gospel genre field was redefined to make a clearer distinction between the traditional gospel music and the style known as Contemporary Christian Music (CCM). As mentioned above, the [Best Roots Gospel Album](/wiki/Best_Roots_Gospel_Album "Best Roots Gospel Album") category is new. The categories in the Gospel field will now be known as *[Best Gospel Performance/Song](/wiki/Best_Gospel_Performance/Song "Best Gospel Performance/Song")*, *[Best Contemporary Christian Music Performance/Song](/wiki/Best_Contemporary_Christian_Music_Performance/Song "Best Contemporary Christian Music Performance/Song")*, *[Best Gospel Album](/wiki/Best_Gospel_Album "Best Gospel Album")*, *[Best Contemporary Christian Music Album](/wiki/Best_Contemporary_Christian_Music_Album "Best Contemporary Christian Music Album")* and *[Best Roots Gospel Album](/wiki/Best_Roots_Gospel_Album "Best Roots Gospel Album")*.

2015 California wildfires :: Nationwide fire season :: chunk_0002
The [National Interagency Fire Center](/wiki/National_Interagency_Fire_Center "National Interagency Fire Center") reported in mid-August that the 2015 fire season had been the most destructive since [2011](/wiki/2011_California_wildfires "2011 California wildfires"). Nationwide, three times as much land, for a total of 6,058,694 acres (24,519 km2), had been burned since the [2014 season](/wiki/2014_California_wildfires "2014 California wildfires").[[8]](#cite_note-accu-8) By the end of August, in terms of the land area burned, the 2015 nationwide wildfire season had surpassed any other wildfire season in the last 10 years, with 7,825,559 acres (31,669 km2) burned.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Hill was born in [Orange, New Jersey](/wiki/Orange,_New_Jersey "Orange, New Jersey"), to [Jamaican](/wiki/Jamaica "Jamaica") parents and was raised in [Sayreville, New Jersey](/wiki/Sayreville,_New_Jersey "Sayreville, New Jersey").[[4]](#cite_note-USAToday-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) He studied ballet at a young age, and appeared in the musical *[The Tap Dance Kid](/wiki/The_Tap_Dance_Kid "The Tap Dance Kid")* as [Savion Glover](/wiki/Savion_Glover "Savion Glover")'s understudy on [Broadway](/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre"), a part he subsequently played on the show's national tour.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Hill graduated from [Sayreville War Memorial High School](/wiki/Sayreville_War_Memorial_High_School "Sayreville War Memorial High School") in 1993,[[8]](#cite_note-sayer-8) and studied business finance at [Seton Hall University](/wiki/Seton_Hall_University "Seton Hall University") and acting at [William Esper Studio](/wiki/William_Esper_Studio "William Esper Studio").[[9]](#cite_note-9) While at Seton Hall,[[8]](#cite_note-sayer-8) he accepted a role on Jim Henson's *[CityKids](/wiki/CityKids "CityKids")*.

Zachary Taylor :: part 03 :: chunk_0002
In 1845, during the [annexation of Texas](/wiki/Annexation_of_Texas "Annexation of Texas"), President [James K. Polk](/wiki/James_K._Polk "James K. Polk") dispatched Taylor to the [Rio Grande](/wiki/Rio_Grande "Rio Grande") in anticipation of a battle with [Mexico](/wiki/Centralist_Republic_of_Mexico "Centralist Republic of Mexico") over the disputed [Texas–Mexico border](/wiki/Mexico%E2%80%93United_States_border "Mexico–United States border"). The Mexican–American War broke out in April 1846, and Taylor defeated Mexican troops commanded by General [Mariano Arista](/wiki/Mariano_Arista "Mariano Arista") at the battles of [Palo Alto](/wiki/Battle_of_Palo_Alto "Battle of Palo Alto") and [Resaca de la Palma](/wiki/Resaca_de_la_Palma "Resaca de la Palma"), driving Arista's troops out of [Texas](/wiki/Texas "Texas"). Taylor then led his troops into Mexico, where they defeated Mexican troops commanded by [Pedro de Ampudia](/wiki/Pedro_de_Ampudia "Pedro de Ampudia") at the [Battle of Monterrey](/wiki/Battle_of_Monterrey "Battle of Monterrey"). Defying orders, Taylor led his troops further south and, though severely outnumbered, repelled Mexican forces under General [Antonio López de Santa Anna](/wiki/Antonio_L%C3%B3pez_de_Santa_Anna "Antonio López de Santa Anna") at the [Battle of Buena Vista](/wiki/Battle_of_Buena_Vista "Battle of Buena Vista"), forcing a withdrawal but without a clear-cut victory. Taylor's troops were transferred to the command of Major General [Winfield Scott](/wiki/Winfield_Scott "Winfield Scott"), but Taylor retained his popularity.

The [Whig Party](/wiki/Whig_Party_(United_States) "Whig Party (United States)") convinced a reluctant Taylor to lead its ticket in the [1848 presidential election](/wiki/1848_United_States_presidential_election "1848 United States presidential election"), despite his unclear political tenets and lack of interest in politics.
